provenance.other: “fellowship one with another” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Helaman 6:3 turns the noun into a verb — 'they did fellowship one with another' — which is a nineteenth-century usage the KJV does not have.
provenance.significance: 1 John 1:7 makes the fellowship conditional and gives it a ground: 'if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship one with another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin.' Helaman 6:3 is the one verse in the chapter where Nephites and Lamanites are one people, and it stands between 6:2, where the Nephites reject the word, and 6:16, where they begin to grow wicked again — so the fellowship lasts exactly as long as the walking in the light does. The whole chapter is then an argument for 1 John's conditional, run in narrative: 6:34's summary, 'the Nephites did begin to dwindle in unbelief … while the Lamanites began to grow exceedingly in the knowledge of their God', is the fellowship dissolving from one side.

6:3.note: A KJV singleton verbed. Held at moderate because four words and a change of part of speech is thin, and 'fellowship one with another' had independent currency in nineteenth-century church language — but the KJV has it once, and the chapter's structure follows the condition attached to it there.
6:3.whyNot: Four words, and the phrase was common enough in Protestant devotional English by 1830 that it need not have come from 1 John at all. Nothing else in Helaman 6 touches the epistle.
6:3.text: But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship one with another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin.

provenance.route: Ephesians 5:1 + Revelation 14:4 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “followers of God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ephesians 5:1, 'Be ye therefore followers of God, as dear children'. “and to the Lamb” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 14:4, of the firstfruits 'unto God and to the Lamb' — the same verse whose second sentence is 'these are they which follow the Lamb whithersoever he goeth'. Helaman 6:5's 'the humble followers of God and the Lamb' joins the two.
provenance.significance: Revelation 14:4 is the only KJV verse that both names following the Lamb and pairs God with the Lamb as a single object, and it is about the hundred and forty-four thousand redeemed from among men. Ephesians 5:1 supplies the phrase 'followers of God' and the reason — 'as dear children'. Fusing them produces a title the KJV does not have and the Book of Mormon uses repeatedly, and the fusion is exact: the noun comes from Paul, the compound object from John. What Helaman adds is 'humble', which is the word the chapter will need again at 6:39, where the Gadianton government tramples 'the poor, and the meek, and humble followers of God'. The title is coined in the verse about conversion and spent in the verse about persecution.

6:5.note: 'To be the humble followers of God and the Lamb.' Two KJV singletons in five words, from two books, joined into a standing Book of Mormon title. Neither phrase is remarkable alone; that both are singletons and that they are adjacent is the evidence.
6:5.text: Be ye therefore followers of God, as dear children;

provenance.other: “buy and sell, and get gain” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “get gain” alone occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Helaman 6:8 reads 'for to buy and to sell, and to get gain, according to their desire' — James's three verbs in James's order, with the infinitive marker repeated.
provenance.significance: James 4:13 is the merchant's sentence — 'To day or to morrow we will go into such a city, and continue there a year, and buy and sell, and get gain' — and James's answer is that he does not know what shall be on the morrow, 'for what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away.' Helaman 6:8 gives the merchant's programme to two nations at peace with each other, and the chapter is the answer: by 6:15 the chief judge is murdered, by 6:17 the search for gain has become secret murder, and by 6:40 they are 'ripening for an everlasting destruction'. Helaman 4:13 had already used the other end of the same passage, James 4:16's 'boastings'. That the book returns to James 4 twice in three chapters — once for the boasting and once for the getting of gain — is a fact about this narrator, and it is the passage that supplies both the sin and the sentence on it.

6:8.note: A KJV singleton reproduced with its three verbs intact. Filed as a quotation on the rarity rather than the length (CONVENTIONS §2); it is far below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and the whole source clause is only six words long. Its weight comes from the batch: Helaman 4:13 borrowed 'boastings' from James 4:16, and this verse borrows the merchant's programme from James 4:13, so the two links are two halves of the same paragraph of James used eighty verses apart.
6:8.text: Go to now, ye that say, To day or to morrow we will go into such a city, and continue there a year, and buy and sell, and get gain:

provenance.other: “toil not, neither do they spin” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. 'Toil' occurs in only four KJV verses in all, and 'spin' in two — Matthew 6:28 and its Lukan parallel at 12:27 — so the pairing of the two verbs is effectively Matthew's alone. Helaman 6:13 has them affirmed: 'their women did toil and spin, and did make all manner of cloth'.
provenance.significance: Matthew 6:28's lilies are the argument against taking thought for raiment: they toil not, neither do they spin, and yet Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of them. Helaman 6:13 is a prosperity notice — the women toil and they spin and they make fine twined linen 'to clothe their nakedness' — and it stands in a passage (6:9-13) that is nothing but the taking of thought Matthew forbids: gold, silver, precious ore, grain in abundance, flocks and herds and fatlings. The inversion is exact and the chapter says what comes of it three verses later: 'the people began to grow exceeding wicked again.' Helaman 5:8 had already used Matthew 6, borrowing 'lay up for yourselves' from 6:20 for a warning against boasting; here the same sermon returns as the description of what the warning did not prevent.

6:13.note: A KJV singleton negated into its opposite. The two verbs are individually rare in the KJV and occur together in one verse; that Helaman puts them together in a catalogue of accumulated wealth, in a book that has already borrowed from the same chapter of Matthew at 5:8, is the argument. The phrase 'to clothe their nakedness' is the Book of Mormon's own and has no KJV source.
6:13.whyNot: Toiling and spinning are what women did, and a writer describing cloth-making would reach for both verbs without Matthew. The link rests on the KJV's own rarity for the pair and on the chapter's setting, not on any shared clause.
6:13.text: And why take ye thought for raiment? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin:

provenance.other: “set not your heart upon” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 62:10: 'Trust not in oppression, and become not vain in robbery: if riches increase, set not your heart upon them.' Helaman 6:17 has the prohibition performed: 'they began to set their hearts upon their riches'.
provenance.significance: Psalm 62:10 names three things in one verse — oppression, robbery, and riches increased — and forbids the heart's attachment to the third. Helaman 6:17 supplies all three in the same order and in the affirmative: the Lord had blessed them with the riches of the world, they set their hearts upon their riches, and they began 'to commit secret murders, and to rob, and to plunder, that they might get gain'. The Psalm's 'become not vain in robbery' is the verse's other half and it is the whole subject of the chapter from here to the end. What makes the borrowing pointed rather than decorative is the causal chain Helaman builds out of the Psalm's list: the Psalm merely juxtaposes robbery and riches, and Helaman makes the second produce the first.

6:17.note: A KJV singleton in the affirmative, in the verse that turns the chapter from prosperity to the Gadianton band. The 1 Timothy 6:9-10 passage ('they that will be rich fall into temptation … the love of money is the root of all evil') is the New Testament's version of the same doctrine and may be fused in, but it supplies no wording; the Psalm supplies the clause and the sequence.
6:17.text: Trust not in oppression, and become not vain in robbery: if riches increase, set not your heart upon them.

provenance.route: Genesis 3:1-6 → Book of Mormon (by reference, not by wording)
provenance.other: No wording is shared. 'Forbidden fruit' is not a KJV phrase — Genesis 3 has 'the tree which is in the midst of the garden' — and 'entice' occurs in Genesis 3 not at all. Hardy's apparatus cross-references Genesis 3:1-5 at this verse; the reference is right and it is a reference to an episode, not to a form of words. Revelation 12:9 is the KJV verse that identifies the serpent with the Devil, which is the identification Helaman 6:26 presupposes.
provenance.significance: Helaman 6:26-29 is a genealogy of one agent through four episodes — Eden, Cain, Babel, Gadianton — held together by the repeated formula 'that same being'. Genesis 3 is the first term and the only one the Book of Mormon does not name outright; it says 'our first parents' and 'the forbidden fruit' rather than Adam, Eve or the serpent, which is what makes the reference allusive rather than expository. The point of putting Eden at the head of the list is what the list is for: secret oaths. The chapter's claim is that a conspiracy of silence is the oldest of temptations, and that its first instance was a promise about knowledge — 'God doth know that in the day ye eat thereof, then your eyes shall be opened' — which is the same structure as Gadianton's secret words at 6:22.

6:26.note: Hardy cross-references Genesis 3:1-5 here and this catalogue agrees with him about the passage while disagreeing about its type: there is no verbal contact whatever, so the row is discharged as a figural link rather than an allusion (CONVENTIONS §6a, third bullet). What is borrowed is an episode and an identification — that the tempter of Eden and the tempter of Gadianton are one being — and the identification itself is Revelation 12:9's, not Genesis's.
6:26.whyNot: Not one word is shared with Genesis 3. If the verse's phrase 'that same being who did entice our first parents to partake of the forbidden fruit' were removed, nothing in the chapter would point to Eden at all; the link exists because the verse makes the reference, not because the text carries it.
6:26.text: Now the serpent was more subtil than any beast of the field which the LORD God had made. And he said unto the woman, Yea, hath God said, Ye shall not eat of every tree of the garden?

provenance.other: “put into the heart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 13:2: 'the devil having now put into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon's son, to betray him'. The KJV's other formulas are 'put in my heart' (Nehemiah 2:12, 7:5, of God) and 'put in their hearts' (Revelation 17:17, also of God). Helaman 6:26 has 'they were put into the heart of Gadianton, by that same being', and the formula then repeats at 6:28 ('who put it into the hearts of the people') and 6:29 ('who put it into the heart of Gadianton'), three times in four verses. The n-gram stream ranked John 13:2 at 6:26.
provenance.significance: John 13:2 is the KJV's one sentence in which the devil puts something into a man's heart, and what he puts there is a betrayal to be carried out in secret by a member of the inner group. Helaman 6:26 uses the construction to explain the origin of the Gadianton oaths, and 6:22 has already described what those oaths are for: secret signs and secret words by which a brother knows a brother, so that 'whatsoever wickedness his brother should do, he should not be injured by his brother'. That is a covenant of mutual non-betrayal, founded — the verse says — by the agency that produced the KJV's one act of betrayal. The metalepsis runs the other way too: Judas is the brother who did tell.

6:26.note: A KJV singleton, used three times in four verses, and used each time to name the agency behind a conspiracy. The formula is what holds 6:26-29 together, and it is the only phrase in that passage with a demonstrable KJV source — the Eden, Cain and Babel references around it are episodic, not verbal. Filed at 6:26 as the first occurrence; 6:28 and 6:29 are registered as recurrences.
6:26.text: And supper being ended, the devil having now put into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon’s son, to betray him;

provenance.other: “of that wicked one” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “slew his brother” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — the same verse, 1 John 3:12. Genesis 4:8 narrates the murder — 'Cain rose up against Abel his brother, and slew him' — and says nothing about who prompted it. 1 John 3:12 is the KJV's one verse that assigns it an author: 'Not as Cain, who was of that wicked one, and slew his brother.' Helaman 6:27's claim, 'that same being who did plot with Cain, that if he would murder his brother Abel, it should not be known unto the world', is 1 John's, not Genesis's; the Book of Mormon keeps Genesis's 'his brother' and takes the wicked one from the epistle.
provenance.significance: 1 John 3:12 sits inside an argument about brotherhood — 'we should love one another. Not as Cain' — and the Gadianton covenant at Helaman 6:22 is a parody of exactly that: a band whose members call each other brother and whose oath is that a brother shall not be injured by a brother. Helaman 6:27 adds to 1 John one element the KJV does not have anywhere: secrecy. Cain's murder is to be a thing 'not known unto the world', which turns the first fratricide into the first secret combination and makes the chapter's whole thesis genealogical. John 8:44's 'he was a murderer from the beginning' stands behind 6:29's 'he hath brought it forth from the beginning of man'.

6:27.note: The verse makes a claim about Cain that Genesis does not make and that one KJV verse does. The wording contact is short — 'his brother', the wicked one as agent — but the proposition is 1 John 3:12's proposition, and the chapter's formula 'that same being' is doing the work of John's 'that wicked one'.
6:27.text: Not as Cain, who was of that wicked one, and slew his brother. And wherefore slew he him? Because his own works were evil, and his brother’s righteous.

provenance.other: Genesis 11:4 reads 'let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven'; Helaman 6:28 reads 'to build a tower sufficiently high that they might get to Heaven'. The shared words are 'build', 'tower' and 'heaven' — the irreducible minimum for naming the episode at all — so the paraphrase is deliberate and no version-specific wording is in view. Hardy's apparatus cross-references Genesis 11:4 at this verse. Genesis 11:8-9's scattering abroad 'upon the face of all the earth' stands behind 'led on the people which came from that tower, into this land'.
provenance.significance: Genesis 11 gives the tower no author but the builders themselves, and no motive but a name and a fear of being scattered. Helaman 6:28 supplies an author — 'that same being' — and thereby folds Babel into the chapter's genealogy of secret works, between Cain and Gadianton. The consequence Helaman draws is the one Genesis leaves implicit: the scattering that Genesis records as punishment becomes, here, the means of transmission, since the being who prompted the tower 'led on the people which came from that tower, into this land'. Babel is how the conspiracy crossed the ocean. That is also the Book of Mormon's own account of the Jaredites, so the verse is at once a biblical allusion and an internal cross-reference.

6:28.note: A paraphrase, not a quotation: the Book of Mormon reproduces the episode and drops Genesis's phrasing entirely, which is why kjvSpecific is 'uncertain' — 'build a tower … get to Heaven' would read the same in any English Bible. Hardy cross-references Genesis 11:4 here and the reference is exact.
6:28.text: And they said, Go to, let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven; and let us make us a name, lest we be scattered abroad upon the face of the whole earth.

provenance.other: “works of darkness” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Romans 13:12 ('cast off the works of darkness, and let us put on the armour of light') and Ephesians 5:11 ('have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them'). The phrase runs three times through this passage — 6:28 'the works of darkness and abominations', 6:29 'the work of darkness, and of secret murder', 6:30 'his works of darkness and secret murder' — and each time it is paired with secrecy.
provenance.significance: Ephesians 5:11's clause is the more apt of the two, since it commands that the works of darkness be reproved and brought to light, and the whole Gadianton apparatus exists to prevent exactly that — 6:24 makes revealing the band's wickedness 'unto the world' a capital offence under 'the laws of their wickedness'. Romans 13:12 supplies the antithesis Helaman does not state: darkness cast off and armour of light put on, at a night far spent. Neither verse can be isolated on the wording, which is why this is filed as an echo; what is worth recording is that the KJV's two-verse phrase becomes this passage's refrain, and that both KJV verses attach the phrase to concealment rather than to sin in general.

6:29.note: Two words with a two-verse KJV home, repeated three times in three verses. Not enough to name a source with confidence, and enough to say that the passage's governing phrase is a KJV phrase used in the KJV's own sense.
6:29.whyNot: 'Works of darkness' is available from either of two verses and had wide currency in nineteenth-century preaching; neither Romans 13 nor Ephesians 5 shares anything else with the chapter.
6:29.text: The night is far spent, the day is at hand: let us therefore cast off the works of darkness, and let us put on the armour of light.

provenance.other: “turn from the holy commandment” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Peter 2:21, whose first clause is 'it had been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness'. “the way of righteousness” occurs in five KJV verses and is not decisive alone; the n-gram stream ranked Matthew 21:32 here on it. What settles the source is the sequence: 2 Peter 2:21 has the way of righteousness known and then the commandment turned from, and Helaman 6:31 has 'turned out of the way of righteousness, and did trample under their feet the commandments of God'. “to his own way” is a KJV singleton at Isaiah 53:6, behind 'did turn unto their own ways'.
provenance.significance: 2 Peter 2:22 completes the sentence with the KJV's two proverbs of relapse — the dog returned to his own vomit and the sow to her wallowing in the mire — which are the same two animals as Matthew 7:6's dogs and swine, and Matthew 7:6 is the verse this chapter borrows twice, at 6:31 and at 6:39. So the two New Testament passages standing behind Helaman 6:31 share their bestiary, and both are about holy things given to those who will not keep them. What Helaman adds is the golden calf: 'did build up unto themselves idols of their gold and their silver' recalls Exodus 32:8, where Israel 'turned aside quickly out of the way which I commanded them: they have made them a molten calf' — the same two motions, out of the way and into an idol, in the same order. Helaman 4:21 had already taken 'stiffnecked people' from the next verse of Exodus 32.

6:31.note: 'Turned out of the way of righteousness … and did turn unto their own ways, and did build up unto themselves idols of their gold and their silver.' A KJV singleton ('turn from the holy commandment') recast as 'trample under their feet the commandments of God', in 2 Peter's own order, with Isaiah 53:6's singleton supplying the middle clause and Exodus 32:8 the shape of the whole. The trampling itself belongs to Matthew 7:6 and is adjudicated at 6:39, where both halves of that verse appear together.
6:31.text: For it had been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness, than, after they have known it, to turn from the holy commandment delivered unto them.

provenance.other: “hardness of their hearts” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 3:5; Matthew 19:8 has 'hardness of your hearts' and Mark 16:14 'hardness of heart'. The Book of Mormon uses each in its correct grammatical setting throughout, and Helaman 6:35 — a narrator's third-person report — takes the third-person form. The n-gram stream ranked Mark 3:5 first in this verse.
provenance.significance: Mark 3:5 is Jesus in the synagogue looking round on the Pharisees 'with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts', immediately before the healing that makes them plot to destroy him. The grief is the point: the KJV's one use of this exact phrase attaches it to a divine reaction, not to a human condition. Helaman 6:35 does the same — 'the spirit of the Lord began to withdraw from the Nephites, because of the wickedness and the hardness of their hearts' — and the withdrawal is the narrator's version of Mark's grief. The verse also completes an arc begun at Helaman 4:24, where the Spirit withdrew for the first time in this book; there the reason was an unholy temple, here it is a hard heart, and 6:36 answers both by pouring the same Spirit out on the Lamanites.

6:35.note: A KJV singleton with the pronoun the setting requires (ADJUDICATING §4). Adjudicated many times from 1 Nephi 2:18 onward and written here because Helaman is a new book and because this occurrence is one half of a matched pair with 6:36 — the Spirit withdrawn from one people in Mark's words and poured out on the other in Joel's, in consecutive verses.
6:35.text: And when he had looked round about on them with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts, he saith unto the man, Stretch forth thine hand. And he stretched it out: and his hand was restored whole as the other.

provenance.other: “pour out my spirit upon” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Joel 2:28. Acts 2:17 quotes the same oracle with a partitive — 'I will pour out OF my Spirit upon all flesh' — and Helaman 6:36 has no partitive: 'the Lord began to pour out his spirit upon the Lamanites'. tools/mediation-check.py run on Joel 2:28 against Acts 2:17 reports no decisive divergence, exactly as it did at Mosiah 25:24 and Alma 16:16, because the divergence is a single common word and the tool suppresses those by design (ADJUDICATING §4). The argument was made in full at Mosiah 25:24 and is not repeated here.
provenance.significance: What makes this occurrence worth a row of its own is the chapter before it. Helaman 5:40-48 is a Pentecost — the crowd's 'what shall we do', the answer 'repent', the Spirit coming down from heaven, fire, and marvellous words — built on Acts 2. Acts 2:16-18 is Peter identifying that event as Joel's oracle, in the partitive form. So when Helaman 6:36 reports the outcome of the prison Pentecost, the natural quotation is Peter's, and the text gives Joel's instead: the same oracle, in the Old Testament's own words, with the whole Spirit rather than a portion of it. The two chapters therefore take opposite routes to one prophecy, and the mediation is the finding.

6:36.note: Joel's clause in the third person and without Peter's partitive, which is what settles the mediation as direct-OT. Paired with 6:35's Mark 3:5 in consecutive verses: withdrawn from the Nephites in the Gospel's words, poured out on the Lamanites in the prophet's.
6:36.text: And it shall come to pass afterward, that I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions:

provenance.other: “under their feet” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “turn again and rend” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — the same verse, Matthew 7:6: 'lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you'. Helaman 6:39 has both halves in one sentence: 'they did trample under their feet, and smite, and rend, and turn their backs upon the poor, and the meek, and humble followers of God.'
provenance.significance: This is the fullest use of Matthew 7:6 in the Book of Mormon and the only one that reproduces both of its verbs. Matthew's sentence is about giving a holy thing into the keeping of animals that will destroy it and then turn on the giver; its subject is the swine, and its object in the second clause is you. Helaman 6:39 collapses the two clauses onto a single object — the poor and the meek are both what is trampled and what is rent — which converts a warning about misplaced trust into a description of class violence. The verse's own governing word makes the substitution explicit: what is trampled is 'humble followers of God and the Lamb', the title coined at 6:5 out of Ephesians 5:1 and Revelation 14:4. So the holy thing in this version of Matthew 7:6 is a group of people. Helaman 4:22 had trampled the laws of Mosiah and Helaman 6:31 the commandments of God; by 6:39 the object is human.

6:39.note: Both halves of a verse each of whose halves is a KJV singleton, in one sentence, with Matthew's own sequence. This is the third and last use of Matthew 7:6 in this batch of chapters — 4:22 (the laws), 6:31 (the commandments), 6:39 (the poor) — and the progression from text to person is the argument. Written as a link rather than a recurrence because the second half of Matthew's verse appears here and nowhere else in the book.
6:39.text: Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you.
